blocks.x: The suburban numbers

[CBRE's Q3 2026 Winnipeg office figures](https://www.cbre.com/insights/figures/winnipeg-office-figures-q3-2026) showed suburban vacancy at 9.7%, compared with 15.1% overall. All of the roughly 28,000 square feet then under construction was suburban, at The District at Bridgwater. For flex space in Winnipeg, [CBRE said](https://mktgdocs.cbre.com/2299/635166d3-3766-4bba-836b-1640e9e191dc-610961676/Winnipeg_Office_Figures_Q3_202.pdf) future supply was focused on suburban flex-office, with Waters Business Park and The Refinery District in the pipeline.
CBRE tied rising suburban rents to demand for high-quality suburban space. Convenient locations, easy parking and space that can serve more than one purpose are likely part of the appeal.
Why flex space appeals in Winnipeg
Flex space combines office areas with warehouse, workshop or showroom space under one roof. It can suit many kinds of business:
Trades and service companies that need an office plus storage for vehicles and equipment.
Distributors and wholesalers with sales offices and inventory.
Professional services firms that want easy parking and a convenient location.
Medical, dental and wellness providers who want accessible, ground-floor space.

Industrial space was tight. Winnipeg industrial availability was 3.1% in [CBRE's Q3 2026 figures](https://mktgdocs.cbre.com/2299/85cf799d-8904-4d62-841f-540174867002-2006882353/Winnipeg_Industrial_Figures_Q3.pdf), or 2.8% within city limits. That can keep pressure on space that offers both office and warehouse functions.
Our view: build for adaptability

The businesses leasing suburban space today will change over the next decade. Some will grow, some will shrink, some will be replaced by tenants with different needs. The most valuable buildings will be the ones that can adapt without major reconstruction.
For suburban flex buildings, new or renovated, that means:
**Open floor plates** with minimal fixed walls, so layouts can change.
**Durable, easy-to-replace finishes** (vinyl plank or polished concrete floors, scrubbable paint).
**Generous entrances and doors** that handle both people and deliveries.
**Demisable units**, so a building can serve one large tenant or several small ones.
**Good daylight**, through well-placed windows and glazed entrances.
Converting older suburban buildings
Not every suburban opportunity requires new construction. Many older suburban office or light-industrial buildings can be updated:
**Interior demolition** to remove outdated offices and open up space, after [testing any suspect materials](/blog/asbestos-testing-before-renovating-manitoba).
**New entrances and storefronts** to create a professional front of house.
**Flooring, painting and lighting** to modernize the office area.
**Window and door replacements** to improve comfort and appearance.
**Masonry repair** to address the exterior.
A conversion starts with a building and a location that already exist, which is worth weighing against building new.
What business owners should consider
For tenants and owner-occupiers thinking about suburban space:
**Calculate total occupancy cost,** not just rent. Parking, utilities and commuting matter.
**Think about growth.** Can the space expand, or can you sublease part of it?
**Budget for fit-out.** Flex space often needs office improvements to suit a specific business.

**Check zoning and permits** for your intended use, especially for customer-facing businesses. A change of use starts with a building permit application, then an occupancy permit; see [occupancy permits and change of use](/blog/occupancy-permit-change-of-use-winnipeg).
Questions to ask before you build or convert

Before starting a suburban office or flex project, owners and developers should test their assumptions. Who are the likely tenants, and what size of space do they need? Is the site zoned for the mix of uses you are planning?
How much parking will tenants and customers need? What is the realistic lease-up period in the target submarket? And how will the building adapt if the first tenant leaves?
For conversions, add a few more. What condition is the existing envelope in? How much interior demolition is needed? Are entrances and doors suitable for the new uses?
What to watch

The suburban advantage may not last. CBRE's Q3 figure was itself a swing from negative suburban absorption in Q2 2026, and if downtown vacancy falls significantly as [Portage Place](/blog/portage-place-redevelopment-downtown-buildings) and other projects progress, the gap may narrow.
In its Q3 2026 figures, CBRE pointed to strong demand for modern suburban space, with little new supply under construction, so well-located and well-finished buildings may continue to lease well.
A note on costs

Suburban flex projects are exposed to the same cost pressures as other construction. Winnipeg construction costs rose by 4% or more in 2025, [Altus Group's 2026 Cost Guide insights](https://www.altusgroup.com/insights/caution-in-2026-optimistic-for-2027-cost-guide-insights/) said, with metals the main material story.

Flex buildings often use steel framing, metal cladding and large overhead doors, and Altus's national highlights tied metal cost increases to US tariffs and trade uncertainty. Owners should confirm pricing early, order long-lead items first and keep contingencies realistic.
The bottom line

On CBRE's Q3 2026 figures, suburban office in Winnipeg was outperforming downtown, and future supply was focused on flex-office. Owners and developers who build or convert with adaptability in mind should be better placed for the next decade.
